::: {.callout-note title="What you'll learn"}
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

1. Say how AI, machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI fit inside
   each other, with an example of each.
2. Explain, using eGFR as the worked example, what it means for a formula to be
   *learned from data* rather than worked out from theory, and name its
   predictors, its response, and the population it was learned from.
3. Tell supervised from unsupervised learning by asking what the training data
   contains, and classification from regression by asking what kind of answer
   the model gives.
4. Say why a model's performance on data it has already seen tells you nothing
   useful, and why separate training and test data is the least you should
   accept.
5. Describe in plain words what a language model computes at each step. Use
   that description to explain why a made-up citation reads exactly like a
   real one.
6. Ask a chatbot to check its own facts and citations, and say what that
   check does and does not catch, including why ChatGPT Edu cannot check facts
   about your patient.
:::

**Time.** About 30 minutes of reading (two of them moving the curve-fitting
sliders), 27 minutes of watching, 25 minutes of doing, and 6 minutes for the
check and the closing question. No math and no
coding are assumed. The only equations in the chapter are one you already use
and a simpler one you can fit by hand with two sliders.
You need a browser and your institutional ChatGPT Edu or Microsoft Copilot
account, or whatever assistant your school provides. Nothing installs, and nothing asks you for a phone number.
The live session uses a [slide deck](../slides/core-foundations.html) with the
same material, and some of the figures there are interactive.

## The number nobody measured

Pre-operative clinic, your surgery sub-internship. A 62-year-old woman is being
worked up for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Her basic metabolic panel is
back, and one line is flagged.

::: {.lab-report}
<div class="hdr">Basic metabolic panel · collected 07:12</div>
<table>
<tr><td>Sodium</td><td>139</td><td></td><td>136–145 mmol/L</td></tr>
<tr><td>Potassium</td><td>4.1</td><td></td><td>3.5–5.1 mmol/L</td></tr>
<tr><td>Creatinine</td><td>1.10</td><td></td><td>0.50–1.10 mg/dL</td></tr>
<tr><td>eGFR (CKD-EPI 2021)</td><td>57</td><td class="flag">L</td><td>&gt;60 mL/min/1.73 m²</td></tr>
</table>
<div class="fine">Illustrative panel, made up for this chapter; not a real patient's result.</div>
:::

The attending asks whether her kidneys are all right for the contrast CT the
surgeon wants. You answer the way everyone answers: "eGFR 57, stage 3a, mildly
reduced, probably fine with hydration." The attending nods. That is the whole
conversation. You will have it several hundred times in intern year.

Now the question at the center of this chapter. Nobody measured her glomerular
filtration rate. Measuring it means infusing a marker that the kidney filters
and does nothing else with, such as inulin or iohexol, and timing how fast it
clears. That takes hours, and it is done almost only in research studies. The
57 on the panel was *computed* from three things the lab did have: her
creatinine, her age, and her sex. Something turned those three numbers into a
kidney function. You trusted it enough to clear her for contrast.

Where did that formula come from? Not from physiology. Nobody worked it out
from the physiology of nephrons. It was **learned from data**. A few
thousand people did have their GFR measured. Their creatinine, age, and sex
were fed to a computer with one instruction: find the formula that best
predicts the measured number. The eGFR is a model. It is the model you already
trust most, and you have never once asked what it was trained on.

Remember this patient. She weighs 45 kilograms and has lost a good deal of
muscle over a year of on-and-off illness. We will come back to her.

## Why this matters

In three months you will meet a dozen of these. A sepsis alert that fires
in the EHR. A risk score that decides who gets a phone call after discharge. A
scribe that drafts your note. A chatbot that answers a dosing question at 2
a.m. Every one of them is the same kind of object as the eGFR: a formula
learned from some population, applied to your patient, with failures that
follow from how it was built. This chapter does not teach you to build these
things. It teaches you to look at one and predict how it will fail, in the
thirty seconds before you act on it.

The second half of the chapter does this for the language model in
particular, because its failures are the strangest and the smoothest. It will
give you a citation that does not exist, formatted perfectly. It will do so
for a reason that follows directly from what it computes. Once you can say
that reason out loud, "it hallucinates" stops being an empty phrase. It becomes a
prediction about when to check.

## How it works

### Four words, each inside the one before

Four words are often used as if they meant the same thing. Each is one kind
of the one around it (@fig-circles). **Artificial intelligence** is a computer
doing a task that seems to need judgment, by any method, even rules written by
hand. **Machine learning** learns its rules from data. The eGFR equation,
which a statistician would call a regression, is an example. **Deep learning**
is machine learning with a **neural network**: many layers of simple units,
each passing numbers to the next. **Generative AI** is deep learning that
writes text or makes images. The large language model behind a chatbot is one
kind. This chapter starts in the second circle and ends in the smallest.

![Four words, each inside the one before. The examples are MYCIN (1970s) for AI, the eGFR equation for machine learning, a chest X-ray reader for deep learning, and a chatbot for generative AI. Drawn for this course.](../images/ai-nested-circles.svg){#fig-circles fig-alt="Four nested circles. The largest is artificial intelligence: a computer doing a task that seems to need judgment, such as MYCIN in the 1970s, whose rules were written by hand. Inside it is machine learning: the rules are learned from data, such as the eGFR equation. Inside that is deep learning: machine learning with many layers, a neural network, such as a model that reads chest X-rays. The smallest is generative AI: deep learning that writes new text or makes images, such as a chatbot."}

### A formula learned from data

The eGFR your lab reports almost certainly uses the CKD-EPI 2021 equation. Here
is how it was made. Researchers combined ten studies in which 8,254 people had
their GFR measured directly with a filtration marker. Each person also had a
creatinine measured by a standard method, an age, and a sex on record. The
researchers then fit an equation that predicts the measured GFR from those
three inputs as closely as possible across all 8,254 people. "Fit" means a
computer tried numbers in the equation until the predictions were as close to
the measured values as they could get. They then tested the equation on a
separate set of 4,050 people from twelve other studies, whose measured GFR the
equation had never seen [@pmid:34554658].

That paragraph contains every term you need for the rest of the course. Here
they are, named:

- **Predictors** are the inputs: creatinine, age, sex. The literature also
  calls them features or variables.
- The **response** is the thing being predicted: measured GFR. Also called the
  label, the outcome, or the truth.
- The **training set** is the 8,254 people whose predictors and response were
  used to fit the equation. The **test set** is the 4,050 people the equation
  was checked on afterwards.
- The **model** is the equation itself, once fit: `eGFR = f(creatinine, age, sex)`.
  The *f* is whatever shape the fitting settled on. For CKD-EPI it is a handful
  of exponents and multipliers. For the systems later in this chapter it is
  billions of numbers. The role is the same.

You can try fitting yourself. Each dot below is one made-up person, with
creatinine across and measured GFR up. The curve is a simple equation with
two numbers in it, *a* and *b*, and the two sliders set them. Each thin line
is a miss: the distance between one person's measured GFR and the curve. Move
the sliders until the average miss is as small as you can make it. Then press
**Show the best fit**.

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// Plain HTML controls for this chapter's two interactive figures, so the page
// needs no input library. Copied from the foundations slide deck.
function rangeInput({ label, min, max, step, value }) {
  const form = html`<form class="w-range" onsubmit="return false"><label><span>${label}</span><input type="range" min="${min}" max="${max}" step="${step}" value="${value}" aria-label="${label}"><output>${value}</output></label></form>`;
  const input = form.querySelector("input"), out = form.querySelector("output");
  form.value = +input.value;
  input.addEventListener("input", () => { form.value = +input.value; out.textContent = input.value; });
  return form;
}
```

```{ojs}
dialData = {
  let s = 20261014;
  const rand = () => { s = (s + 0x6d2b79f5) | 0; let t = Math.imul(s ^ (s >>> 15), 1 | s);
    t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t; return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296; };
  const gauss = () => Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(1 - rand())) * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * rand());
  return Array.from({ length: 40 }, () => { const cr = 0.6 * Math.pow(4 / 0.6, rand()); return { cr, gfr: 80 * Math.pow(cr, -1.1) * Math.exp(0.15 * gauss()) }; });
}
dialCurve = (a, b) => cr => a * Math.pow(cr, -b)
dialMiss = (a, b) => { const f = dialCurve(a, b); return dialData.reduce((t, p) => t + Math.abs(f(p.cr) - p.gfr), 0) / dialData.length; }
// The best fit, found by trying every setting the two sliders allow.
dialBest = {
  let best = { a: 0, b: 0, miss: Infinity };
  for (let a = 30; a <= 150; a++) for (let k = 0; k <= 40; k++) { const b = +(k * 0.05).toFixed(2), miss = dialMiss(a, b); if (miss < best.miss) best = { a, b, miss }; }
  return best;
}
```

```{ojs}
  const W = 640, H = 400, l = 64, r = 14, t = 12, b = 54, ymax = 170;
  const X = cr => l + (cr - 0.5) / 3.5 * (W - l - r), Y = g => H - b - Math.min(g, ymax) / ymax * (H - b - t);
  const f = dialCurve(dialA, dialB);
  const grid = Array.from({ length: 141 }, (_, i) => 0.5 + i * 0.025);
  const path = "M" + grid.map(c => `${X(c).toFixed(1)},${Y(f(c)).toFixed(1)}`).join("L");
  return html`<svg class="wchart" viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${H}" role="img" aria-label="Forty made-up people, creatinine against measured GFR, with the curve for a ${dialA} and b ${dialB}. Average miss ${dialMiss(dialA, dialB).toFixed(1)}.">
    ${[0, 40, 80, 120, 160].map(v => `<line class="grid" x1="${l}" x2="${W - r}" y1="${Y(v)}" y2="${Y(v)}"/><text class="tick" x="${l - 8}" y="${Y(v) + 6}" font-size="17" text-anchor="end">${v}</text>`).join("")}
    ${[1, 2, 3, 4].map(v => `<text class="tick" x="${X(v)}" y="${H - b + 24}" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle">${v}</text>`).join("")}
    ${dialData.map(p => `<line class="miss" x1="${X(p.cr).toFixed(1)}" x2="${X(p.cr).toFixed(1)}" y1="${Y(p.gfr).toFixed(1)}" y2="${Y(f(p.cr)).toFixed(1)}"/>`).join("")}
    ${dialData.map(p => `<circle class="dot" cx="${X(p.cr).toFixed(1)}" cy="${Y(p.gfr).toFixed(1)}" r="5"/>`).join("")}
    <path class="curve" d="${path}"/>

}
```

<p class="eq">GFR = <b>a</b> × creatinine<sup>−<b>b</b></sup></p>

```{ojs}
viewof dialA = rangeInput({ label: "a", min: 30, max: 150, step: 1, value: 50 })
viewof dialB = rangeInput({ label: "b", min: 0, max: 2, step: 0.05, value: 0.3 })
```

<p class="defn"><b>a</b>: the GFR when creatinine is 1.0. <b>b</b>: how fast GFR falls as creatinine rises.</p>

```{ojs}
{
  const miss = dialMiss(dialA, dialB), best = dialA === dialBest.a && dialB === dialBest.b;
  return html`<div class="readout" role="status"><span class="test">Average miss: <b class="dial-miss">${miss.toFixed(1)}</b> mL/min/1.73 m²</span></div>
    ${best ? html`<div class="fb ok">The best fit: no setting of a and b misses by less.</div>` : ""}`;
```

```{ojs}
{
  const button = html`<button class="w-btn" type="button">Show the best fit</button>`;
  button.onclick = () => {

      const input = view.querySelector("input");
```

<p class="src">● one made-up person · thin line: how far the curve misses that person · thick line: the curve your sliders make. Generated in your browser.</p>
:::

**Fitting** means a computer does exactly this until the error is as small as
it can get. Here the computer tries every setting the sliders allow and keeps
the best one. Real fitting uses faster methods with the same goal. The real
eGFR equation has a few more numbers in it, and it was fit to 8,254 people
whose GFR was measured, not to 40 made-up dots.

@fig-egfr-proxy shows what that model connects. The thing you want to know is
on the right. The thing the lab can measure is on the left. The equation is
the bridge, and the bridge was built from a specific set of people.

A number used in place of the one you want, because that one is hard to get,
is called a **proxy**. The first of the course's four recurring lessons (the
fourth, *who benefits, who bears the risk, who decides*, comes in
[the ethics chapter](core-ethics-regulation.qmd)) is **proxies fail**: the stand-in and the real thing can come apart,
and they come apart for some patients more than for others. [The bias and
equity chapter](core-bias-equity.qmd) depends on that lesson. This chapter's
job is narrower: to show you the bridge at all.

Three things follow from "learned from data". Each one is a question you can
ask of any model.

**The truth column existed.** For every one of the 8,254 people, someone had
actually measured the real GFR. That is what makes this
**supervised learning**: the training data contains the answer, and the model
learns to reproduce it. **Unsupervised learning** is what you do when there is
no answer column, only patterns to find. Sorting 10,000 tumor expression
profiles into groups, without being told which are which, is unsupervised. The
test is simple: does the training data contain the thing you want predicted?

**The model gives a number.** eGFR is a quantity, so this is **regression**:
the output is a value on a scale. If the same inputs were used to output "CKD:
yes or no", that would be **classification**: the output is a category. Most
clinical prediction tools are one or the other, and the difference decides how
you judge them. A regression is wrong by an amount. A classification is wrong
by a *kind*, a miss or a false alarm, and those two kinds cost different people
different things.

**The model is exactly as good as the people it was fit to.** The 8,254 came
from research studies and clinical populations, and 31.5 percent of them were
Black. All were adult outpatients without serious other illness; none were
children [@pmid:34554658]. None were your patient. For anyone outside that
set, the equation is guessing beyond what it saw. Statisticians call that
guess an *extrapolation*. The history of the equation is a history of finding
out where the guess failed; the box "If you have more time", later in this
section, tells it.

### The loop, in general

Every model in this course, from the eGFR to the chatbot, was built by the
same loop. @fig-loop draws it once.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-loop
%%| fig-alt: "Flowchart. Raw material such as labs, images, notes, or text becomes predictors; the truth for each case, such as measured GFR, sepsis yes or no, or the next word, joins them in a learning step that finds a function f so that truth is approximately f of predictors; the result is a model, and a new case with unknown truth goes through the model to produce a prediction."
%%| fig-cap: "The loop every learned model comes from. Turn the raw material into predictors, collect the truth for each case, learn a function that predicts truth from predictors, then apply it to a case whose truth you do not have. The eGFR, a sepsis alert, and a language model differ only in what fills the boxes."
flowchart LR
  accTitle: The loop every learned model comes from
  accDescr: Flowchart. Raw material such as labs, images, notes, or text becomes predictors. The truth for each case, such as measured GFR, sepsis yes or no, or the next word, joins them in a learning step that finds a function f so that truth is approximately f of predictors. The result is a model, and a new case with unknown truth goes through the model to produce a prediction.
  raw[Raw material:<br/>labs, images, notes, text] --> pred[Predictors]
  truth[Truth for each case:<br/>measured GFR, sepsis yes/no,<br/>the next word] --> learn
  pred --> learn["Learn: find f so that<br/>truth ≈ f(predictors)"]
  learn --> model["Model: response = f(predictors)"]
  new[New case, truth unknown] --> model --> ans[Prediction]
```

You now have two questions that sort any model in about ten seconds. They are
the ones the Check asks you to apply:

| Question | If yes | If no |
|---|---|---|
| Does the training data contain the answer? | Supervised | Unsupervised |
| If supervised: does the model give a category? | Classification | Regression (a number) |

: Two questions that sort any model. {#tbl-two-questions}

### Why performance on data it has seen tells you nothing

Here is the mistake the eGFR researchers avoided, and the one every vendor
slide invites you to make. Suppose you fit a formula to 8,254 people. Then you report
how well it predicts GFR *in those same 8,254 people*. You have measured how
well the formula memorized them, not how well it will work on the next
patient. A flexible enough model can fit its training data perfectly and be
useless. Its performance on data it has already seen is not evidence. It is a
description of the fitting.

![Every one of these fits the same data. The one on the bottom right passes through every point, and it is the worst model of the twelve. xkcd 2048, *Curve-Fitting*, by Randall Munroe, [CC BY-NC 2.5](https://xkcd.com/license.html) (non-commercial use only).](../images/curve_fitting.png){#fig-xkcd-curve .comic fig-alt="xkcd comic: a grid of twelve scatterplots of the same data, each with a different fitted curve and a caption, from a straight line labeled linear, through quadratic and logarithmic, to a wildly wiggling curve labeled 'connecting lines' with the caption 'I clicked a button and this came out', and one labeled 'house of cards' that fits every point."}

That is why separate training and test sets are the least you should accept.
You fit on one set of cases. You report performance on a *different* set the
model never saw. The 4,050-person validation set in the eGFR paper is that
second set. When a claim about a model gives you one number and does not say
which set it came from, you do not yet have a number.

There are two ways to get this wrong. A model that is **too simple** misses
the real pattern: the straight line through a curve. A model that is **too
flexible** learns the random scatter in its training cases along with the
real pattern, so it fits those cases closely and the next case badly: the
wiggle through every point. You will see both with one slider in Part A of
the Do.

The clinical version of the same failure is **dataset shift**: the patients
the model meets in real use differ from the patients in its training set, so
performance measured during development does not hold [@pmid:34260843].
Here is an example. One EHR vendor built a sepsis model that was in use at
hundreds of US hospitals in 2021. One academic center tested it on its own 38,455
hospitalizations, in a setting the model was not built on. A test
like that is called *external validation*; here the testers also had no part
in building the model. The model had an area under the
curve of 0.63, on a scale where 0.5 is no better than chance and 1.0 is perfect. It
missed 67 percent of patients with sepsis, and it alerted on 18 percent of all
admissions [@pmid:34152373]. Nobody had lied about the development
performance. It simply had not been measured on patients like those. So a
test set protects you only if it looks like the patients you will use the
model on.

::: {.callout-important title="The one sentence"}
A model's performance on the cases it was built from is usually the optimistic
number. That is the third of the course's four recurring lessons, **the
published number is the optimistic one**, in its first form. Ask what it was
trained on, and ask what it was tested on. If those
are the same set, you have learned nothing yet. If the test set does not look
like your patients, you have learned less than the number suggests.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="If you have more time: when a good result did not carry over"}
**The eGFR equation, three times.** Each version was learned from a
population, and each one's known failure is in people outside it.

| Equation | Year | Learned from | Tested on | What broke, and where |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MDRD | 1999 | 1,628 patients with chronic kidney disease, of whom 1,070 were the training sample | The remaining 558 | Fit to people with reduced GFR; gave values that were too low at higher GFR, so healthy people were labeled as diseased [@pmid:10075613; @pmid:19414839] |
| CKD-EPI | 2009 | 8,254 participants in 10 studies | 3,896 in 16 studies | More accurate at higher GFR, but included a term that adjusted the result for Black race. The 2021 study found that the equation with this term overestimated measured GFR in Black adults by a median of 3.7 mL/min/1.73 m²; with the term simply removed, it underestimated by 7.1 [@pmid:19414839; @pmid:34554658] |
| CKD-EPI 2021 | 2021 | 8,254 participants in 10 studies, refit without race | 4,050 in 12 studies | Now recommended for all US laboratories; the refit without race still gives values a few mL/min too low in Black adults and a few mL/min too high in non-Black adults, and a cystatin C version is more accurate [@pmid:34554658; @pmid:34563581] |

: Three generations of the eGFR equation, rebuilt from the numbers in the papers. {#tbl-egfr-history}

Every row says the same thing: *the model was fit to these people, and here is
what happened to other people.* The training population is a property of the
model, as much as the equation is. [The bias and equity
chapter](core-bias-equity.qmd) takes up why the race term was there and who
was harmed by it.

**Chest X-rays and COVID-19.** A separate test set is necessary, but it is
not enough. Early in the pandemic, many groups built models to label a chest
X-ray as COVID-19 or not. A review of 62 such papers found that 16 took their
non-COVID images from one public set of pneumonia X-rays from children aged
one to five, while the COVID-19 images came from adults. In the reviewers'
words, a model built this way "is likely to overperform as it is merely
detecting children versus adults" [@doi:10.1038/s42256-021-00307-0].

DeGrave and colleagues rebuilt models of this kind, with the COVID-19 and
non-COVID X-rays from different sources [@doi:10.1038/s42256-021-00338-7].
On a test set held back from the same sources, the models did well. On
radiographs from a new hospital system, in the authors' words, "half of the
model's predictive performance is lost". @fig-covid-average shows one reason:
the sources differ in places that have nothing to do with the disease.
@fig-covid-saliency shows that the models used those places, such as side
markers, image edges, and the diaphragm. When the authors swapped the side
markers between a COVID-19 X-ray and a non-COVID X-ray, the model's output
shifted.

Solid boxes mark side markers that differ between sources. Dashed boxes mark differences in how dark the image edges are. Dashed red boxes outline the dark top corners and side edges of every image, which differ in darkness between sources. Solid red boxes mark a side marker visible in the top-left of PadChest and a faint letter R on the left of BIMCV-COVID-19+."}

![What the model looked at. Left, three chest X-rays. Right, a *saliency map* for each: the pixels that most changed the model's answer, darker red for more influence. Top, a non-COVID X-ray: the model used the lungs (open arrow) but also the side marker in the top corner (closed arrow). Middle, a COVID-19 X-ray: the strongest pixels are in the bottom corners, outside the lungs. Bottom, a COVID-19 X-ray: the only highlighted area is the diaphragm. From DeGrave, Janizek and Lee (2020), Figure 2a, cropped from the full figure, medRxiv preprint [@doi:10.1101/2020.09.13.20193565], [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); image from [PubMed Central](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7523163/).](../images/covid-xray-saliency-degrave-2020.jpg){#fig-covid-saliency fig-alt="Three chest X-rays on the left, labelled COVID-19 negative, COVID-19 positive, and COVID-19 positive, each beside a speckled red map on the right. Arrows on the maps point to a side marker in the top-right corner of the first image, to the two bottom corners of the second, and to the diaphragm in the third. A colour bar runs from 0th percentile, white, to 99th percentile, dark red."}

The test set came from the same mixed sources as the training set, so it had
the same flaw and could not catch it. The literature calls this *shortcut
learning*. An epidemiologist would call the source a *confounder*: a third
factor linked both to the image and to the label. When you read a claim like
this, ask where each group of images came from.

**MYCIN and Watson.** MYCIN, a rule-based system for choosing antimicrobials
built at Stanford in the 1970s, was evaluated blind by eight experts on ten
meningitis cases. Its acceptability rating, 65 percent, was higher than that
of any of the five faculty specialists it was compared with [@pmid:480542].
It was never used in routine patient care [VERIFY: a source that MYCIN never
entered clinical use; the cited evaluation does not say]{.verify}. IBM Watson
went from winning *Jeopardy!* in 2011 to a cancer-center collaboration that
was set aside in 2017 after an audit, without entering clinical use
[@pmid:30053147]. Neither story argues that today's tools will fail. Both
show that a striking result is not the same as a tool in use on the ward.
:::

### From tables to words

Everything so far had a table: one row per patient, one column per predictor,
one column of truth. A language model is the same loop with a different table.
Seeing that is the key point.

Take any sentence from the internet: *the patient was started on empiric*.
Split it into **tokens**, which are words or pieces of words. "Empiric" might
be one token and "vancomycin" three. Now the predictors are the tokens so far,
and the truth is the very next token. You do not need anyone to label
anything, because the next word is already in the text. Every
sentence ever written becomes a training case, with no labeling work. That is why these
models could be trained on a very large fraction of the written internet.

To make tokens usable by the loop, each one is turned into a list of numbers,
called an **embedding**. The numbers are chosen so that tokens used in similar
contexts get similar numbers. "Vancomycin" ends up near "linezolid" and far
from "Tuesday". That is the "raw material to predictors" box of @fig-loop,
done for words.

The model is then trained to do one thing: given the tokens so far, produce a
probability for every possible next token. Then one token is picked, at random
but weighted by those probabilities. It is added to the end, and the process
runs again. A paragraph of smooth medical prose is a few hundred repetitions
of *predict the next token, pick one, repeat*. Your phone's keyboard suggests
the next word the same way, with a small model that looks back only a few
words. Chatbots do it at a much larger size. In 2026 a typical large model
works with a vocabulary of about a hundred thousand tokens or more, looks back
over many thousands of tokens, and has billions of numbers in its *f*. The
exact sizes change with each new model. The video shows what happens inside.
What matters here is what the process does not contain.

There is a second training stage, and it explains the tone. After the
next-token training, people are paid to compare pairs of answers and say which
one they prefer. The model is then adjusted toward the preferred kind. The
literature calls this reinforcement learning from human feedback. It is what
turns a text-completer into an assistant that answers your question, in
paragraphs, politely. It also means the model has been trained toward answers
people *rate well*, which is not the same as answers that are true. In
practice it tends to reward confidence and completeness, because a cautious,
incomplete answer loses those comparisons. A general review for clinicians of
how these chatbots are built, and of the mixed results so far, is a good next
read [@pmid:37460753].

Now the main sentence of the chapter:

::: {.callout-important title="Nothing in this process checks whether a claim is true"}
At no step does the model look anything up, consult a database, or compare a
statement to the world. It produces the most plausible next token, meaning the
one most likely to follow, given the tokens so far and given what people rated
well. A real citation and a made-up one are both plausible ways to continue
"the original paper was". The model is not lying, and it is not broken. It is
doing exactly what it was built to do, and the thing it was built to do has no
truth step in it. Today's chatbots can add a check on top of this process if
you ask for one; [Ask it to check](#ask-it-to-check), below, shows how.
:::

Here is what that looks like when it reaches you. The exchange below is
illustrative, made up for this chapter. The scoring system, the point values
it gives, and the reference are the kind of thing a model produces, not a
transcript.

::: {.chat}
<div class="user">What are the exact point values and cutoffs for the HEART score, and what is the original publication?</div>
<div class="bot">The HEART score assigns 0–2 points each for History, ECG, Age, Risk factors, and Troponin, for a total of 0–10. Patients scoring 0–3 are low risk (about 1.7% risk of a major adverse cardiac event at 6 weeks) and can be discharged; 4–6 is intermediate (about 12–17%); 7–10 is high risk (about 50–65%) and warrants early invasive management.<br/><br/>Original publication: Backus BE, Six AJ, Kelder JC, et al. "A prospective validation of the HEART score for chest pain patients at the emergency department." <em>Int J Cardiol.</em> 2013;168(3):2153–2158.</div>
<div class="fine">Illustrative exchange, made up for this chapter. Do not use it as a source for the HEART score.</div>
:::

Read it as a clinician and it is fine. Read it knowing how the model works,
and every clause is a plausible continuation. The structure is right. The
names are real people who have written about this score. The journal exists.
But is the *original* publication the one named? Are the percentages from that
paper, or a later one, or nowhere? Do the cutoffs match what MDCalc shows?
The model did not check any of that, because checking is not a step. You will
find out in the exercise. The first description of the score is in fact in a
different journal and year [@pmid:18665203]. That is exactly the kind of
detail that a smooth continuation gets *almost* right.

::: {.callout-note title="What this does and does not mean"}
It does not mean the answer is usually wrong. On common questions these models
are right most of the time, because the most plausible continuation of a
well-documented fact is the fact. It means the *error rate is not zero and the
tone does not change when it is wrong.* A made-up citation reads exactly like
a real one. That is the justified part of the fear. The outdated part is the
belief that the tools are unreliable for everything. [The critical appraisal
chapter](core-appraisal.qmd) measures the rates. This chapter explains why there is a rate at all.
:::

### Ask it to check

The model itself has no checking step. Most chatbots now have web search built
in. It was added to deal with two problems: the training data stops at a date,
called the *training cutoff*, and the model can make things up. Search lets the
chatbot compare a claim to a real source, and you can ask it to. Add this to
your question, or send it after the answer:

```{.script}
Check each fact and citation in your answer using web search. For each one, give a link (PubMed or the DOI) and a short quote from the source that supports it. Mark anything you could not find.
```

Three studies say what a check like this does and does not do.

- **Search helps.** One 2026 study asked six chatbot versions for references
  on ear, nose, and throat topics. The two versions with web search gave more
  accurate references than the four without it. The best scored 51 percent
  on the study's reference-accuracy rating [@pmid:41546380].
- **A second pass helps.** In another study, a model wrote questions to check
  its own first draft, answered them separately, and then rewrote the answer.
  The rewritten answers made fewer false claims [@doi:10.18653/v1/2024.findings-acl.212].
- **Neither makes it perfect.** In a 2025 study of medical questions, a chatbot
  with web search still gave about 3 statements in 10 that the source it cited
  did not support [@pmid:40240349]. A real link is not the same as a link that
  says what the answer says.

There is also a limit no search can fix. ChatGPT Edu cannot see the chart;
some tools built into the electronic health record can. So ChatGPT Edu cannot
check facts about your patient: the dose against the patient's weight, the
history against the notes. Those are yours to check.

So let the chatbot check the literature. Then open the link yourself before
anything goes in a note or an order.

probability for every possible next word, picks one, and repeats. Then it is

## Do

::: {.callout-warning title="No patient information, ever"}
All three parts of this exercise use public or made-up material. Part A runs
on made-up data in your browser. Parts B and C ask the model about a published
scoring system, not about a patient. Your university ChatGPT Edu or Copilot
account, signed in with university credentials, is covered by a business
associate agreement, the contract that makes the vendor legally responsible
for protecting patient data. That covers patient care. This exercise is not
patient care. The question you will be
tempted to ask about the patient from this morning is one you do not ask. And
whatever drafts a note, you sign it. What to document when a tool helped is
[the ethics chapter's](core-ethics-regulation.qmd) question.

### Part A: overfitting you can see (5 minutes)

The slider below fits a curve to twelve made-up cases, the filled dots. Sixty
more cases, the hollow dots, are held back as a test set; the model never
learns from them. The dashed line is the real pattern, which the model never
sees. The slider sets how flexible the model is. At 0 the curve is a flat
line, at 1 a straight line, and each step to the right lets it bend more.

Under the charts are two numbers. The **training error** is a kind of average
miss on the cases the model learned from. The **test error** is the same
average miss on the held-back cases. That pair of numbers is the point of the
exercise. The chart on the right shows both errors at every setting, and a
vertical line marks where the slider is.

Move the slider slowly from 0 to 11. Stop at 0, at 3, and at 11, and write
down both errors each time.

```{ojs}
bvData = {
  let s = 20261003;
  const rand = () => { s = (s + 0x6d2b79f5) | 0; let t = Math.imul(s ^ (s >>> 15), 1 | s);
    t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t; return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296; };
  const gauss = () => Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(1 - rand())) * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * rand());
  const truth = x => Math.sin(3 * x);
  const make = n => Array.from({ length: n }, () => { const x = rand() * 2 - 1; return { x, y: truth(x) + 0.3 * gauss() }; });
  return { truth, train: make(12), test: make(60) };
}

// Least squares in a Legendre basis, solved by modified Gram-Schmidt QR.
function basis(x, d) { const p = [1, x]; for (let k = 1; k < d; k++) p.push(((2 * k + 1) * x * p[k] - k * p[k - 1]) / (k + 1)); return p.slice(0, d + 1); }
function fitPoly(pts, d) {
  const m = pts.length, n = d + 1, Q = pts.map(p => basis(p.x, d)), R = Array.from({ length: n }, () => Array(n).fill(0));
  for (let j = 0; j < n; j++) {
    for (let i = 0; i < j; i++) { let dot = 0; for (let r = 0; r < m; r++) dot += Q[r][i] * Q[r][j]; R[i][j] = dot; for (let r = 0; r < m; r++) Q[r][j] -= dot * Q[r][i]; }
    let nrm = 0; for (let r = 0; r < m; r++) nrm += Q[r][j] ** 2; nrm = Math.sqrt(nrm); R[j][j] = nrm; for (let r = 0; r < m; r++) Q[r][j] /= nrm || 1;
  }
  const qtb = Array.from({ length: n }, (_, j) => pts.reduce((a, p, r) => a + Q[r][j] * p.y, 0)), c = Array(n).fill(0);
  for (let i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) { let v = qtb[i]; for (let k = i + 1; k < n; k++) v -= R[i][k] * c[k]; c[i] = R[i][i] ? v / R[i][i] : 0; }
  return x => basis(x, d).reduce((a, v, k) => a + v * c[k], 0);
}
rmse = (f, pts) => Math.sqrt(pts.reduce((a, p) => a + (f(p.x) - p.y) ** 2, 0) / pts.length)
bvErrors = Array.from({ length: 12 }, (_, d) => { const f = fitPoly(bvData.train, d); return { d, train: rmse(f, bvData.train), test: rmse(f, bvData.test) }; })
bvFit = fitPoly(bvData.train, degree)
```

::: {.widget}
<div class="illus-label">Illustrative: made-up data, generated in your browser.</div>

```{ojs}
viewof degree = rangeInput({ label: "Flexibility of the model", min: 0, max: 11, step: 1, value: 1 })
```

:::: {.widget-pair}
```{ojs}
{
  const W = 600, H = 340, p = 14;
  const x = v => p + (v + 1) / 2 * (W - 2 * p), y = v => H / 2 - Math.max(-3, Math.min(3, v)) / 2.2 * (H / 2 - p);
  const grid = Array.from({ length: 241 }, (_, i) => -1 + i / 120);
  const path = f => "M" + grid.map(v => `${x(v).toFixed(1)},${y(f(v)).toFixed(1)}`).join("L");
  const now = bvErrors[degree];
  return html`<svg class="wchart" viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${H}" role="img" aria-label="Fitted curve at flexibility ${degree}: training error ${now.train.toFixed(2)}, test error ${now.test.toFixed(2)}.">
    <path class="truth" d="${path(bvData.truth)}"/>
    ${bvData.test.map(d => `<circle class="test-dot" cx="${x(d.x).toFixed(1)}" cy="${y(d.y).toFixed(1)}" r="4"/>`).join("")}
    ${bvData.train.map(d => `<circle class="dot" cx="${x(d.x).toFixed(1)}" cy="${y(d.y).toFixed(1)}" r="6.5"/>`).join("")}
    <path class="curve" d="${path(bvFit)}"/>
  </svg>`;
}
```

```{ojs}
{
  const W = 520, H = 340, l = 64, r = 16, t = 16, b = 50, cap = 1.5;
  const X = d => l + d / 11 * (W - l - r), Y = e => H - b - Math.min(e, cap) / cap * (H - b - t);
  const line = key => "M" + bvErrors.map(e => `${X(e.d).toFixed(1)},${Y(e[key]).toFixed(1)}`).join("L");
  const off = bvErrors.some(e => e.test > cap);
  const now = bvErrors[degree];
  return html`<svg class="wchart" viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${H}" role="img" aria-label="Error by flexibility. Training error falls steadily. Test error falls, then rises${off ? " off the chart" : ""}. At flexibility ${degree}: training ${now.train.toFixed(2)}, test ${now.test.toFixed(2)}.">
    ${[0, 0.5, 1, 1.5].map(v => `<line class="grid" x1="${l}" x2="${W - r}" y1="${Y(v)}" y2="${Y(v)}"/><text class="tick" x="${l - 8}" y="${Y(v) + 8}" font-size="24" text-anchor="end">${v.toFixed(1)}</text>`).join("")}
    <line class="marker" x1="${X(degree)}" x2="${X(degree)}" y1="${t}" y2="${H - b}"/>
    <path class="train-line" d="${line("train")}"/>
    <path class="test-line" d="${line("test")}"/>
    ${off ? `<text class="test-label" x="${W - r}" y="${t + 40}" font-size="24" text-anchor="end">test error off the chart ↑</text>` : ""}
    <text class="axis" x="${(l + W - r) / 2}" y="${H - 12}" font-size="26" text-anchor="middle">more flexible →</text>
    <text class="axis" x="20" y="${(t + H - b) / 2}" font-size="26" text-anchor="middle" transform="rotate(-90 20 ${(t + H - b) / 2})">error</text>
  </svg>`;
}
```
::::

```{ojs}
{
  const now = bvErrors[degree];
  return html`<div class="readout" role="status"><span class="train">● Training error ${now.train.toFixed(2)}</span><span class="test">○ Test error ${now.test > 1.5 ? "above 1.5" : now.test.toFixed(2)}</span></div>`;
}
```

<p class="src">● cases the model learns from (the training set) · ○ cases held back for testing (the test set) · dashed line: the real pattern, which the model never sees · solid line: the model's curve.</p>
:::

Then write three sentences, and keep them. You will need them for the Check.

```
Which setting was too simple, and how could you tell?
______________________________________________________________

Which setting was too flexible, and how could you tell?
______________________________________________________________

If you had only seen the training error, which setting would you
have picked, and what did the test error show?
______________________________________________________________
```

The third sentence is the one you will use again. It is the same question you
will ask of every performance figure on every vendor slide for the rest of
your career.

### Part B: produce a hallucination on purpose (15 minutes)

Pick one scoring system from @tbl-scores in a specialty you have rotated
through, so that you already know roughly what the right answer is. Each row's
original publication has been checked in PubMed for this chapter, so you have
a verified target.

| Specialty | Score | Original publication (verified) |
|---|---|---|
| Emergency medicine | HEART score | Six, Backus, Kelder. *Neth Heart J* 2008 [@pmid:18665203] |
| Internal medicine, pulmonology | CURB-65 | Lim et al. *Thorax* 2003 [@pmid:12728155] |
| Surgery | Alvarado score | Alvarado. *Ann Emerg Med* 1986 [@pmid:3963537] |
| Psychiatry, primary care | PHQ-9 | Kroenke, Spitzer, Williams. *J Gen Intern Med* 2001 [@pmid:11556941] |
| Gastroenterology | Glasgow-Blatchford score | Blatchford, Murray, Blatchford. *Lancet* 2000 [@pmid:11073021] |
| Oncology | ECOG performance status | Oken et al. *Am J Clin Oncol* 1982 [@pmid:7165009] |
| Pediatrics, obstetrics | Apgar score | Apgar. *Curr Res Anesth Analg* 1953;32:260–267, [PMID 13083014](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/13083014/) (a 1953 record with no DOI, so it is linked rather than cited) |
| Any medicine service | Wells score for PE | Wells et al. *Thromb Haemost* 2000 [@pmid:10744147] |

: Eight scoring systems with their original publications, each confirmed in PubMed on 2026-09-07. Pick the one you know best. {#tbl-scores}

Open your chatbot in a fresh conversation and ask:

> Give me the exact point values and cutoffs of the `<score>`, the outcome
> each cutoff was validated against, and the full original publication that
> first described it: first author, journal, year, volume, and pages.

Now verify, in this order. Open the score on [MDCalc](https://www.mdcalc.com)
and compare every point value and cutoff. Then open PubMed, search the first
author and year the model gave you, and compare against @tbl-scores. Use
PubMed and not Google Scholar. Scholar's loose matching will show you a
different real paper for a citation that does not exist, and you will score it
as found.

Large current models usually get this right for scores this well known. If
yours did, ask a second question in the same conversation:

> Give me five references, with PubMed IDs, that support `<a claim from the
> score's original paper>`.

Open each PMID in PubMed and read the title. A wrong PMID usually opens a real
paper about something else, so a link that works proves nothing. When the
course tested four models with this question on 3 October 2026, every one of
them gave at least one wrong PMID.

Record:

```
Tool and model version if shown: ____________________________
Score chosen: ______________________________________________

Point values and cutoffs: all correct / one wrong / more than one wrong
  What was wrong, exactly: _________________________________

Original publication as given by the model:
  ____________________________________________________________
  Matches the verified original?  Y / N / partly (which fields differ)

Second question, if you asked it:
  PMIDs whose title matched the paper described: ___ of 5
  What the wrong ones opened: ________________________________

How the model produced this, in one sentence, using the words "token"
or "plausible continuation" and not the word "hallucinate":
  ____________________________________________________________
```

The last line is the one that matters. "It made a mistake" is not an
explanation. "It predicted the most plausible next tokens after 'the original
publication was', and a plausible citation looks exactly like a real one" is.
The model may get everything right. If it does, write that down too, and then
write the sentence anyway. A model that is right nine times in ten, with no
change of tone on the tenth, is the more dangerous object. That is why
unverified output is dangerous rather than merely useless. Then, if you have
two minutes left, ask the same thing again in plainer words, the way you would
say it out loud. The answer depends on the wording more than you would expect.
[the critical appraisal chapter](core-appraisal.qmd) measures by how much.

::: {.callout-tip title="If the model refuses or hedges"}
Some assistants will now say they cannot guarantee citations, or will offer to
search the web. A hedge is a design choice added on top of the same process,
and it is worth noting in your record. A tool tuned to hedge has not checked
anything. Asking it to check is Part C.
:::

### Part C: ask it to check (5 minutes)

Stay in the same conversation, and send the prompt from
[Ask it to check](#ask-it-to-check):

```{.script}
Check each fact and citation in your answer using web search. For each one, give a link (PubMed or the DOI) and a short quote from the source that supports it. Mark anything you could not find.
```

Open two of the links it gives. For each one, find the quote on the page and
decide whether the source says what the answer said.

Record:

```
What the check corrected: ___________________________________
What it marked as not found: ________________________________

Link 1: does the source say what the answer said?  Y / N / partly
Link 2: does the source say what the answer said?  Y / N / partly

One thing this check could not catch, and why:
  ____________________________________________________________
```

## What this changes for you

*What does this change about how you'll practice?* Write it down before you
close this chapter.

Then go back to the clinic. The 62-year-old woman is still on the schedule.
She weighs 45 kilograms and has lost muscle over a year of illness, and
creatinine comes from muscle. Look at @fig-egfr-proxy: the grey box feeds the
predictor without touching the truth. Her creatinine of 1.10 is a normal
number for a normal amount of muscle. She does not have a normal amount of
muscle. So the same creatinine probably means a *lower* true GFR than the 57
the equation returned. Was she among the 8,254? What would you ask for
instead? What do you now say to the attending about the number on the panel?
One word is not an answer. And notice that nobody told her a model had a part in
her care either. Whether that matters, and when, is [the patient-communication
chapter's](core-patient-communication.qmd) question, not this one's.

And the second half. The next time a chatbot gives you a citation with a first
author, a journal, and a year, what is the one sentence you will say to
yourself before you paste it anywhere? Will you ask it to check, and which
link will you then open yourself? Which facts in the answer are about your
patient, so that ChatGPT Edu cannot check them for you?

## Summary

- The eGFR is a model learned from data: creatinine, age, and sex in; a
  stand-in for measured GFR out; 8,254 research participants as the
  population it was fit to. Every learned model has those three parts, and you can
  ask for them.
- Supervised learning has the answer in the training data; unsupervised does
  not. Classification gives a category; regression gives a number.
- Fitting means a computer adjusts the numbers in a formula until its error
  on the training data is as small as it can get.
- Performance on the training data describes the fit. It is not evidence.
  Ask for the test set; if there is none, there is no number yet.
- A test set protects you only if it looks like your patients. The COVID-19
  X-ray models scored well on test sets cut from the same flawed sources, and
  lost about half their performance at other hospitals.
- Too simple is bias, too flexible is variance, and a different population is
  dataset shift. All three are failures of the same object.
- A language model turns text into a table where the predictors are the
  tokens so far and the truth is the next one. It predicts, picks one, and
  repeats. Human raters then tune it toward answers people prefer.
- Nothing in that process checks whether a claim is true. A made-up citation
  is a plausible continuation, produced in the same tone as a real one.
- You can ask a chatbot to check its facts and citations with web search. It
  helps, it is not perfect, and it cannot check facts about your patient.
  Open the link yourself.
- The 57 on the panel came from somewhere. So does everything else.

## Go deeper

**Videos and talks**

- 3Blue1Brown, *Transformers, the tech behind LLMs* (Deep Learning, Chapter
  5), 1 April 2024, 27 minutes. <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wjZofJX0v4M>.
  The longer version of the Watch video, with a transcript at
  <https://www.3blue1brown.com/lessons/gpt>. Look for the passage on
  embeddings, where words become directions in space and "woman minus man"
  ends up near "queen minus king". If you cannot follow the section on
  attention, skip it.
- Andrej Karpathy, *Intro to Large Language Models* (November 2023, about one
  hour). <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zjkBMFhNj_g>. More advanced than
  the 3Blue1Brown videos: what the two training stages are, why the second one
  produces an assistant, and a section on prompt injection (tricking a model
  with instructions hidden in the text it reads).
- 3Blue1Brown, *But what is a neural network?* (Deep Learning, Chapter 1).
  <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aircAruvnKk>. For the *f* in @fig-loop,
  if you want to see what is inside a neural network.
  October 2017; 19 minutes.
- Course decks, permanent at the archive:
  [Deep learning intro](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2024-11-06-deep-learning-intro/),
  with medical-imaging examples;
  [Word embeddings as the basis for LLMs](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2024-11-12-word-embeddings-basis-for-llms/),
  which has an Embedding Projector exercise for the "words become numbers"
  step; and [AI history](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2025-09-30-ai-history/),
  for MYCIN and Watson at length.

**Papers**

- The CKD-EPI 2021 development and validation paper. It is a model card (a
  one-page description of a model: what it was trained on, what it was
  tested on, and where it fails) before the term existed: predictors, response, training set, test
  set, and where it is wrong, all in one abstract [@pmid:34554658]. The
  NKF-ASN task force report explains why the refit happened [@pmid:34563581].
- Dataset shift for clinicians, in two pages [@pmid:34260843], and the
  external validation of the vendor sepsis model that is its best-known
  example [@pmid:34152373].
- A primer on how the chatbots are built and what the early clinical results
  look like [@pmid:37460753].
- The review of COVID-19 imaging models that found the children-versus-adults
  problem [@doi:10.1038/s42256-021-00307-0], and the study that showed what
  the X-ray models were looking at instead of the lungs
  [@doi:10.1038/s42256-021-00338-7].
- MYCIN's blinded evaluation, forty-seven years old and still an example of how
  to test a decision-support tool well [@pmid:480542].

**If you want the other algorithms**

This chapter deliberately named no algorithms beyond regression and the neural
network. Random forests, nearest neighbors, and penalized regression are all
the same loop with a different *f*. They are laid out with examples at
<https://seandavi.github.io/RBiocBook/machine_learning/models.html>.
